deep.reconstruction:
Setting: a finite arrangement (a 'système') of pseudolines in the real projective plane, so that any two pseudolines meet exactly once. It is viewed as a combinatorial map ('carte') whose vertices s carry multiplicity ν(s), the number of pseudolines through s. The previous page states the goal: reconstruct the map from combinatorial data K^+. To do this one needs (i) a 'polygonal structure', meaning a cyclic or dihedral order, on the set of arcs leaving each vertex s, and (ii) a canonical choice of one of its two orientations. This page supplies (ii) despite the non-orientability of RP^2.

Definitions. Let \vec{\mathcal D} be the set of oriented pseudolines. Let \vec{\mathcal D}(s) be the set of oriented pseudolines through s. It is in canonical bijection with the arcs (half-edges) of origin s: an arc determines the pseudoline it lies on, oriented away from s. So |\vec{\mathcal D}(s)| = 2ν(s).

For an oriented pseudoline \vec D not through s, define ρ_{\vec D,s} as a cyclic permutation of \vec{\mathcal D}(s): 'turn once around s in the positive sense'.
- The positive sense is fixed by \vec D as follows. RP^2 \ |D| is an open disc (an affine plane). Its closure has a boundary circle that double-covers |D| connectedly, so an orientation of D lifts to the boundary circle and orients the disc.
- Thus an oriented pseudoline determines an orientation of its affine complement, hence a local orientation at every vertex off it, hence a rotation (successor map) on the half-edges at s.

Properties.
- (a) ρ_{-\vec D,s} = ρ_{\vec D,s}^{-1}: reversing D reverses the disc orientation.
- (b) If \vec D, \vec D' do not pass through s, then ρ_{\vec D,s} and ρ_{\vec D',s} are equal or mutually inverse. The underlying cyclic (dihedral) structure at s is intrinsic; only the orientation can differ.
- The crossed-out (c) began to describe how the comparison sign ε(D,D',s) = ±1 varies with s. It is redone on the next page: for s, s' on a third line Δ, the sign is the same iff s, s' lie in the same one of the two segments of Δ cut out by x = Δ∩D and x' = Δ∩D'. Equivalently, ε(D,D',·) is constant on each of the two regions of RP^2 \ (D∪D') and has opposite values on them.
- Next-page (d) links ρ_{\vec D,s} to the order of intersection points along \vec D: the rotation at s corresponds to taking the successor along \vec D among the points where D meets the lines through s.

This is the projective/pseudoline analogue of a rotation system for a map on a non-orientable surface. Instead of edge signatures, one uses a family of local orientations indexed by oriented pseudolines, with an explicit cocycle-like comparison rule.

ideas.what: Oriented pseudolines through a vertex identified with the outgoing half-edges (2ν(s) of them)
ideas.modern_name: darts/half-edges of a map; local sequence at a vertex
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard (combinatorial maps: Tutte, Cori; Goodman–Pollack local sequences)

ideas.what: An oriented pseudoline orients its complement (an affine disc), hence induces a rotation ρ_{D,s} at each vertex off it
ideas.modern_name: orientation of the affine chart RP^2 \ L; rotation system relative to a line at infinity
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore (affine pictures of pseudoline arrangements / oriented matroids, Folkman–Lawrence 1978, Goodman–Pollack)

ideas.what: Comparison of local orientations induced by two lines: constant on each of the two regions of RP^2 minus D∪D', opposite on the two
ideas.modern_name: sign/cocycle comparing orientations of affine charts; related to chirotope sign changes

ideas.what: Program of reconstructing the cellular map of a pseudoline arrangement from combinatorial data (K^+) via polygonal structures at vertices
ideas.modern_name: combinatorial encoding of arrangements (allowable sequences, wiring diagrams, rank-3 oriented matroids) and map encodings
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck's 'cartes' viewpoint appears in Esquisse d'un programme (1984), but not pseudoline arrangements specifically

missed.claim: Grothendieck encodes a map on the non-orientable surface RP^2 by a family of rotations ρ_{D,s} indexed by oriented lines, with explicit transformation rules (inversion, equal-or-inverse, region-dependent sign). This is a variant of signed rotation systems tailored to arrangements. It is a small documentary point showing how he extended his 'carte' formalism (later in Esquisse) to non-orientable/projective settings via pseudolines. It is not a new theorem.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Of historical interest for Grothendieck's c. 1981 combinatorial-topological work on maps and arrangements, which is largely unknown. The mathematics itself is folklore in the oriented matroid / pseudoline literature.

deep.surprise_reason: Correct, careful but elementary foundational setup: local orientations at vertices induced by oriented pseudolines, and their comparison rules. Equivalent facts are folklore in the theory of pseudoline arrangements and oriented matroids. The interest is mainly historical, showing Grothendieck working on pseudoline arrangements as maps around 1981.
